title: Swiatek Battles into Canadian Open Final, Calls Season Her 'Toughest'
summary:
Iga Swiatek, the six-time Grand Slam champion, has had a season she'd rather forget—until this week. On Thursday, she battled past Elina Svitolina 6-3, 1-6, 6-3 in the Canadian Open semi-finals in Toronto, reaching her first WTA final since winning Cincinnati exactly 12 months ago. It's a milestone that seemed distant for much of 2026, a year in which Swiatek had only reached one semi-final before this tournament.

"It hasn't been an easy season, probably the toughest one in my life," Swiatek admitted after the match. "This week has been really positive and inspirational for me, and it always kind of shows that you need to keep going no matter what." The 25-year-old Pole, seeded seventh, had to dig deep after Svitolina dominated the second set. But Swiatek regrouped, using her trademark heavy topspin and relentless defense to close out the match.

Her opponent in Friday's final will be Elena Rybakina, the Australian Open champion and world No. 2. Rybakina also needed three sets, coming from behind to beat Coco Gauff 5-7, 6-2, 6-2. It was her second straight comeback win, having rallied against Naomi Osaka in the quarter-finals. "I'm just glad that I managed to win again in three sets," Rybakina said.

The final will be the 13th meeting between Swiatek and Rybakina, with their head-to-head deadlocked at 6-6. Their only match this year came in the Australian Open quarter-finals, where Rybakina won in straight sets en route to the title. "It's going to again be a very difficult match, and we know each other so well," Rybakina said. "In my case, I feel it's more again about the recovery after so many hours on the court, and bring as much energy as I can."

For Swiatek, a win would be a triumphant end to a challenging season. For Rybakina, it would add another big title to her breakout year. Either way, expect a battle.
why_it_matters: This match is a study in how elite athletes handle prolonged slumps and self-doubt, showing that success is not a straight line. It also highlights the physical and mental recovery demands of top-level tennis, where a single tournament can shift a player's confidence before a major.

background_read: Women's professional tennis is organized around the WTA Tour (the Women's Tennis Association, which runs top-level women's events).

Iga Swiatek (Poland's 25-year-old six-time Grand Slam singles champion) entered this Canadian Open seeded seventh, a rare spot for a player with her record, and had not reached a final since winning Cincinnati exactly 12 months earlier.

The Canadian Open, one of the oldest tennis tournaments in North America, alternates between Toronto and Montreal and is played on hard courts during the summer, just before the U.S. Open, the final Grand Slam of the year.
Elena Rybakina (the Australian Open champion and world No. 2) has become a consistent hard-court threat, and her head-to-head series with Swiatek was tied at 6-6 before this final.
Coco Gauff and Naomi Osaka, both major champions, lost earlier in the same section, underlining the depth of the field.

perspectives.description: Sees the final as proof that persistence through a difficult season pays off. Her ability to regroup after losing the second set shows the mental toughness that made her a multi-time Grand Slam champion.

Worries that long three-set matches and 'so many hours on the court' increase the risk of burnout or injury. Critics may question whether the WTA schedule gives players enough recovery time before high-stakes finals.

The 6-6 head-to-head record and Rybakina's straight-sets win at the Australian Open show how closely matched the two are. The match may turn less on skill than on recovery, energy, and who controls baseline rallies with topspin and depth.

The result could shape the narrative for both players heading into the U.S. Open. A Swiatek win would close a tough season on a high note; a Rybakina win would cement her breakout year and create a new hard-court rivalry dynamic.
